comments.author: @sammysamba
comments.text:
People need to understand why millions of workers are getting paid "minimum wage" even though it's barely enough to make a living. That's the whole point! Let me explain this for Americans who don't understand what minimum wage is for, or foreigners who don't know anything about American economics.

The federal minimum wage is the lowest a company is required to pay an employee in the United States. The reason it is intentionally low is to serve as an incentive for employers so they can afford to hire more people and still turn a profit. Why is this important to the government? They need the tax revenue from businesses, which pay higher taxes overall than individuals.

Now, most people would ask, "Well, why is the government helping employers but not employees?" That's not entirely true either. Just as the government gives employers incentives like low wage requirements and tax breaks, it also provides benefits and assistance to low-income individuals in the form of subsidies. What's that, you ask? Things like public transportation (do you really think $1.50 is what it costs to bus 20 to 30 people around town?), SNAP benefits (food stamps), housing relief (Section 8 vouchers), and free healthcare (Medicaid).

So you see, the government works both ways: it appeases employers by allowing them to pay lower wages, and in return, it offsets the burden on employees by offering subsidized services to make up the shortfall.

The real problem is the middle ground—the middle class—who are the ones getting totally screwed in this poorly thought-out economic structure. The problem for the American middle class is that because household incomes sit above the poverty threshold, they don't qualify for government subsidies (the "freebie handouts") given to low-income households. In other words, low-income households, despite making bare minimum wages, get free groceries, reduced rent, and cheap public transportation to bridge the gap. Middle-class earners don't, and the government has no solution for them!

That's why the middle class in America has shrunk over the last 40 years. Many people either prefer to downgrade their socioeconomic status to receive benefits, or they pursue high-paying careers and business ownership for upward mobility.

The reality today is that most employers in this economy simply cannot afford to provide livable wages like they once did. In fact, that's the sole reason unions became so powerful in America—they could control segments of the workforce to collectively bargain for skilled labor. With recent economic disruptions like COVID-19, international trade conflicts, tariffs, and AI, employers are getting squeezed at every turn to create and maintain high-paying jobs while inflation remains rampant.

The entire system is flawed, right down to the money itself, which is a whole other topic. Bottom line: it is systemically better to be a minimum-wage worker with government benefits in America because the chances of securing a high-paying career with true job security (pensions, retirement, healthcare) or starting a successful business are low-probability outcomes. The majority of available jobs in America pay middle-class wages where employees make just enough to barely cover living expenses—completely cut off from government assistance until they reach 65 and qualify for social services.
